steps.label: Bit-String Flicking
steps.content:
ACSL Junior Contest 2

Bit-String Flicking

Competition

  • Today: change a row of bits with operators, work out long expressions, and solve for x.
  • In the contest: two of the five short questions are on this topic.
Think → Pair → ShareA bit can only be 0 or 1. Why is a row of bits so useful to a computer?Show the answer

Each bit can stand for one thing that is on or off, so one short row can hold many facts at once.

steps.label: Why Flick Bits?
steps.content:
Why Flick Bits?

Think → Pair → SharePredict: a game keeps five settings in one row of five bits. Why is that better than five words like ON and OFF?Show the worked answer

Five bits take far less space than five words.

One operation can check or change all five settings at once.

  • Computers keep on and off settings as bits called flags: 1 is on, 0 is off.
  • A mask is a bit string that picks which bits to keep, change or switch on.
  • Pictures are rows of bits too. Moving every bit one place moves the picture.
  • Bit-string flicking means changing bit strings with operators.

Game settings

steps.label: NOT: Flip Every Bit
steps.content:
NOT: Flip Every Bit

Think → Pair → SharePredict: what is NOT 10110? Why is it the same length?Show the worked answer

NOT 10110 = 01001

Each bit is flipped where it is. No bit is added or taken away.

  • NOT works on one bit string.
  • Every 1 becomes 0. Every 0 becomes 1.
  • The answer has the same number of bits.

Think → Pair → SharePredict all three answers for 11010 and 10011. Why can you work one column at a time?Show the worked answer

AND: 10010. OR: 11011. XOR: 01001.

Each column only uses the two bits in that column. No column changes another.

  • AND with a mask keeps the bits under a 1 and clears the rest.
  • OR with a mask switches on the bits under a 1.
  • XOR with a mask flips the bits under a 1.

steps.label: Check: Four Operators (1 of 2)
steps.content:
Check: Four Operators (1 of 2)

Think → Pair → ShareWhy does AND with a mask clear some bits but never set a new 1?Show the answer

AND needs both bits to be 1, so a 0 in the mask always gives 0, and a 1 in the mask only keeps what was there.

Type each answer as 5 bits.

steps.label: Check: Four Operators (2 of 2)
steps.content:
Check: Four Operators (2 of 2)

Think → Pair → ShareHow can you check an XOR answer once you have it?Show the answer

XOR the answer with the second string. You should get the first string back.

Type each answer as 5 bits.

steps.label: Shifts: Bits Fall Off
steps.content:
Shifts: Bits Fall Off

Think → Pair → SharePredict: what are LSHIFT-2 10111 and RSHIFT-1 10111? Why do zeros appear?Show the worked answer

LSHIFT-2 10111 = 11100 and RSHIFT-1 10111 = 01011.

The string keeps its length, so the empty places at the other end are filled with zeros.

  • LSHIFT-n moves every bit n places left.
  • The first n bits fall off. They are lost.
  • n zeros come in on the right.
  • RSHIFT-n does the same to the right.
  • The length never changes.

Predict

steps.label: Circulates: Bits Wrap Round
steps.content:
Circulates: Bits Wrap Round

Think → Pair → SharePredict: what are LCIRC-2 10111 and RCIRC-1 10111? Why are there no new zeros?Show the worked answer

LCIRC-2 10111 = 11110 and RCIRC-1 10111 = 11011.

No bit is lost. A bit that falls off one end comes back on the other end.

  • LCIRC-n moves every bit n places left.
  • A bit that falls off the left end comes back on the right.
  • RCIRC-n does the same to the right.
  • Nothing is lost, so the number of 1s stays the same.

steps.content:
Compare: LSHIFT-2 and LCIRC-2

Think → Pair → SharePredict both answers for 11001. Which bits are the same in both? Why are the last two different?Show the worked answer

LSHIFT-2 11001 = 00100 and LCIRC-2 11001 = 00111.

The first three bits are the same: they moved the same way. At the right end, the shift brings in zeros, but the circulate brings back the two bits that fell off.

steps.label: Big Counts: Go Round Again
steps.content:
Big Counts: Go Round Again

Think → Pair → SharePredict: what is RCIRC-12 10110? Why do you not need to make 12 moves?Show the worked answer

After 5 moves, 5 bits are back where they started. 12 = 2 × 5 + 2, so it is the same as RCIRC-2.

RCIRC-12 10110 = 10101

  • A circulate of 5 places on 5 bits brings every bit back to the start.
  • So take away 5 as many times as you can. Only the remainder matters.
  • Example: on 5 bits, LCIRC-7 is the same as LCIRC-2.
  • A shift of 5 or more on 5 bits leaves 00000: every bit has fallen off.

steps.content:
Check: Shifts and Circulates (1 of 2)

Think → Pair → ShareWhy must a shift answer always have the same number of bits as the start?Show the answer

Every bit that falls off one end is replaced by a zero at the other end.

steps.label: Check: Shifts and Circulates (2 of 2)
steps.content:
Check: Shifts and Circulates (2 of 2)

Think → Pair → ShareWhy can a circulate never change how many 1s a string has, but a shift can?Show the answer

A circulate brings every bit back on the other end. A shift loses bits and brings in zeros.

Type each answer as 5 bits.

steps.label: Activity 1: Flick Lab
steps.content:
Activity 1: Flick Lab

Think → Pair → ShareWhy does a target round make you plan every move before you run it?Show the answer

You must predict each step in your head, the way you will in the contest, instead of trying buttons until it works.

Predict: set every bit, then Check. Target: plan every move, then Run. Wrong answers cost a life.

steps.label: Which Operator Goes First?
steps.content:
Which Operator Goes First?

Think → Pair → SharePredict: in NOT LSHIFT-1 11010, which operator goes first? Why?Show the worked answer

LSHIFT-1 goes first: it is next to the bits. LSHIFT-1 11010 = 10100, then NOT gives 01011.

The order

  1. NOT (first)
  2. LSHIFT, RSHIFT, LCIRC, RCIRC
  3. AND
  4. XOR
  5. OR (last)
  • Brackets are always worked first.
  • Then go down the list: NOT first, OR last.
  • Two of the same, like AND and AND: work left to right.
  • NOT and the shifts sit in front of their bits. A chain of them works right to left: the one next to the bits goes first.

steps.label: Compare: Left to Right or By the Order?
steps.content:
Compare: Left to Right or By the Order?

Think → Pair → SharePredict: Ana works 10110 OR 01100 AND 00111 from left to right. Ben uses the order. Who is right? Why?Show the worked answer

Ben. AND comes before OR, so 01100 AND 00111 = 00100 first, then 10110 OR 00100 = 10110.

Ana gets 00110: the same bits, a different order, a different answer.

steps.content:
Check: Which Goes First? (1 of 2)

Think → Pair → ShareWhy does the contest need an agreed order for the operators?Show the answer

Without one, two people could work out one expression in two ways, with two different results.

items.prompt: In 11010 XOR 01101 AND 10011, which operator is worked first?
items.explain: AND comes before XOR in the order, wherever it is in the line.

steps.label: Check: Which Goes First? (2 of 2)
steps.content:
Check: Which Goes First? (2 of 2)

Think → Pair → ShareWhy can a wrong first step never be put right later in the working?Show the answer

Every later step uses its result, so the mistake is carried all the way to the end.

items.prompt: In NOT RCIRC-2 01101 OR 10000, which operator is worked first?
items.explain: NOT and RCIRC-2 are a chain in front of the bits. The one next to the bits goes first.

steps.label: Different Lengths
steps.content:
Different Lengths

Think → Pair → SharePredict: what is 101 AND 11011? Where do the missing bits go, and why there?Show the worked answer

Pad 101 to 00101: zeros on the left, so its value stays the same. Then 00101 AND 11011 = 00001.

  • AND, OR and XOR need two strings of the same length.
  • Pad the shorter string with zeros on the left.
  • The answer has the length of the longer string.
  • NOT, shifts and circulates keep the length of their own string.

steps.label: Activity 2: Precedence Pile-up
steps.content:
Activity 2: Precedence Pile-up

Think → Pair → ShareWhy does each step shrink the expression?Show the answer

Each operator and its bits are replaced by one answer, so there is less left to work out.

Click the operator that is worked next, then set its answer. A wrong choice costs a life.

steps.label: A Contest-Style Expression
steps.content:
A Contest-Style Expression

Think → Pair → SharePredict the five steps in order before you work any of them out. Why is NOT not the first step?Show the worked answer
  1. LCIRC-2 10101 = 10110
  2. RSHIFT-1 01110 = 00111
  3. 10110 XOR 00111 = 10001
  4. NOT 10001 = 01110
  5. 01110 AND 11011 = 01010

NOT works on the whole bracket, so the bracket must be finished first.

NOT (LCIRC-2 10101 XOR RSHIFT-1 01110) AND 11011

  • 1. Find the brackets. Work inside them first.
  • 2. Inside, do NOT, shifts and circulates first.
  • 3. Then AND, then XOR, then OR.
  • 4. Write every step on its own line.

Check: Contest-Style Expressions

Think → Pair → ShareWhy is writing every step on its own line worth the time in a contest?Show the answer

One slip early on spoils every step after it. A written step can be checked again quickly.

steps.label: Solve for x: The Mask Hides Some Bits
steps.content:
Solve for x: The Mask Hides Some Bits

Think → Pair → SharePredict: which 5-bit values of x make x AND 10110 = 00110 true? Why can some bits of x be anything?Show the worked answer

Under each 1 in the mask, x must equal the answer bit. Under each 0, AND gives 0 whatever x is, so that bit is *.

x = 0*11*: 4 values (00110, 00111, 01110, 01111).

  • A * means "this bit can be 0 or 1".
  • Go column by column. Ask: which bits of x give the answer bit?
  • AND with 0 always gives 0: x can be anything there.
  • OR with 1 always gives 1: x can be anything there.
  • Each * doubles the number of answers.

x AND 10110 = 00110

mask10110
answer00110
x?????

steps.label: Solve for x: Undo the Circulate
steps.content:
Solve for x: Undo the Circulate

Think → Pair → SharePredict: solve (LCIRC-2 x) OR 01001 = 11101. Why do you undo the circulate last?Show the worked answer

First find what LCIRC-2 x must be: 1*10*. That bracket is the last thing done to x, so it is the last thing to undo.

Undo LCIRC-2 with RCIRC-2, stars and all: x = 0*1*1.

  • Work from the outside in: undo the last operator first.
  • Call the bracket y. Solve y OR 01001 = 11101 column by column.
  • Then undo the circulate: move the pattern back the other way. The stars move too.
  • Test one answer at the end to be sure.

(LCIRC-2 x) OR 01001 = 11101

steps.label: Check: Solve for x
steps.content:
Check: Solve for x

Think → Pair → ShareHow can you check a pattern answer without trying every value?Show the answer

Test one value that fits the pattern, then change one * bit and test again.

x has 5 bits. Use * for a bit that can be 0 or 1.

steps.label: Practice: Find X
steps.content:
Practice: Find X

Think → Pair → ShareWhy is testing one value of x not enough to answer the question?Show the answer

One value can work while others work too. The question asks for every value, so you need the pattern.

Find every x. Use * for any bit. Two free tests, then one Check per puzzle.

Try the Real Thing

The contest has its own wording and layout. Seeing it before the day means no surprises.

  • The ACSL wiki page explains every operator with more examples.
